title: The last words in Pali
hook: a saved voicemail, a last text: the Buddha's last words, and two ways to hear them
tomorrow: dhamma or dharma: which spelling is the right one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sadhu: good, well done, said three times to share in someone else's good. Today, the words a whole tradition has been answering ever since.

Some people keep a voicemail for years because of what it is: the last thing someone said to them. Last words get weighed and replayed. In the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha is lying between two sala trees at Kusinara, near the end. He asks his monks whether anyone has a doubt left, about the Buddha, the teaching, the path. He asks a second time, and a third. Silence. Then he speaks. The text says plainly: these were his last words. And ever since, people have heard them two ways.
screen: `A SAVED VOICEMAIL.` → `BETWEEN TWO SALA TREES.` → `ANY DOUBT LEFT? SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here they are: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha. Vaya, falling away; dhamma, nature; sankhara, things put together. Whatever is put together has the nature to fall apart. Then: appamadena, with appamada; sampadetha, bring it to completion. Rhys Davids gave it this way: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Salvation is his word; the Pali simply says bring it to completion. Now the debate, and it lives inside the tradition. One side hears urgency. Things fall apart, the teacher is leaving, time is short: strive. Don't wait for a better year. That reading has the first half on its side, and the ring of diligence. The other side hears care. Appamada is a negative: not heedless, not careless, and the commentary ties it to mindfulness that never goes missing. Read that way, the last word isn't a whip. It's a steady hand: pay attention, and keep paying it. That reading has the word itself on its side. Both sides chant the same line, and the line can carry both: the push and the attention. Strive on, with care.
screen: `VAYADHAMMA SANKHARA: THINGS FALL APART.` · `APPAMADENA SAMPADETHA: COMPLETE IT.` · `ONE SIDE: URGENCY. STRIVE.` · `THE OTHER: CARE. DON'T GET CARELESS.` · then, large: `STRIVE ON WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back for the sit. On one step, say inwardly vayadhamma sankhara; on the next, appamadena sampadetha. If walking isn't possible, tap it out with your fingers on your knee, one phrase to each tap.
The last words in Pali: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha. Things fall apart; complete the path with care.
screen: `THE LAST WORDS IN PALI — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: strive on with care, the push and the attention together. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your friend reads 'work out your salvation with diligence' and says it means grind until you drop. what's the best case for the other side?
options: appamada is heedfulness: steady attention that never goes missing, not a frantic push.
the last words were only a goodbye, so they don't really ask anything.

fork.reveal: the care reading stands on the word itself, non-heedlessness, and the commentary's link to mindfulness. the urgency reading stands on 'things fall apart'. the line holds both.

original.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: appamadena, with heedfulness; sampadetha, bring it to completion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stern 'work hard' from a dying teacher.
what it means: things put together fall apart, so bring the path to completion with appamada, heedfulness.
what a scholar hears: appamada is a negative, non-heedlessness, so the line can be read as urgency or as care; Rhys Davids' 'salvation' has no match in the Pali.

chat.meaning: Appamadena sampadetha holds both: things pass, so don't waste time, and don't get careless. Strive on, with care.

notes: Rhys Davids (SBE XI, 1881), DN 16 VI.10: 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!' Confirm exact wording and punctuation; the Dialogues II (1910) version differs slightly.
'Salvation is his word; the Pali simply says bring it to completion' (sampadetha) is a translation note, not a comment on any other tradition. Confirm.

Debate shape: urgency vs care. 'The commentary ties appamada to mindfulness that never goes missing' (sati-avippavasa in the commentary on DN 16) is paraphrased; confirm. The teach's last lines say only that the line 'can carry both'; no claim about what most teachers hold.

Gentle line for parents: the scene is the Buddha's death (between two sala trees at Kusinara); kept calm and brief. Day 1439 (the funeral verse) covers the words spoken at his passing, so this day stays on the last words and their two readings.
